reason: Inflorescences are divided or dissected; 'divisée dès la base' fits.
Inflorescence axes and rachis can be angular; the examples fit.
'Few veins' is a count of parts, not a quality of one vein. A counted-parts rule is needed to attach it to the leaf. Compare config/flora_counted_parts.tsv.
A short panicle is meaningful. One example ('rameaux très courts') is about branches, not the panicle.
The part has no label here. Width in metres suggests a whole-plant or crown spread. Allowed only if the FLOPO class is that kind of part.
The examples describe appendices, not the banner petal. This is a wrong part reading.
The examples describe small appendices, not the banner petal itself. This is a wrong part reading.
A banner petal can be densely silky-hairy ('étendard velu-soyeux'). The velutinous term is a slightly loose match for silky.
Hairy is fine for most surfaces, but the part has no label and I could not check what the class is. It needs a check of what FLOPO_0986083 is.
Measured thicknesses ('8 cm thick') belong to thickness with a value, not to 'increased thickness', which is a comparison.

Lobed is meaningful for flat or fleshy parts. The part has no label, and the examples mix lobed with cut into strips. A rule would need to know whether the class is a lobed organ or a part bearing lobes.
Dense foliage or canopy is meaningful, and the examples are consistent.
Lodicules are often described as small or minute.
Bracts can be filiform. Some examples describe an acumen (a tip), not the bract.
'En forme de tuba' means trumpet-shaped, which is not exactly tubular. There is only one example, and the part has no label.
The example is about the orifice of the part, not the part itself. A rule would need an orifice-of-part class.
Dark glands: secretory tissue can be dark-coloured.
'Marginés' means having a distinct margin. PATO 'structure' is a generic attribute and the wrong reading.
'Becoming glabrous with age' is meaningful for surfaces and organs that bear hairs.
Lepidote or scaly fruits are common and the examples are correct.
The examples describe hooked, sigmoid or uncinate pappus bristles, not sickle-shaped (falciform) ones. The PATO term means something else.
Length measurements are meaningful for any measurable part.
Triangular is a normal shape for flat parts, and the examples fit.
A lobe can be subcircular, as in the median lobe example.
Superposed pseudobulb stems (orchids) can be read as stacked, but 'superposées' may also mean overlapping. A rule would need the context (pseudobulbs).
Sagittate sepals are meaningful. 'Sigmoïdes' is a mis-hit from the same stem.
'Attached to' is a relation between two parts, not a quality of the lamina. It belongs in a relation or base-attachment rule.
Trichomes can be pointed, as in a unicellular pointed tip. Some examples are about auricles or the apex.
Shoots and twigs can be quadrangular.
Robust shoots are a normal description.
Shoots can be straight. One example is about prickles.
'Introrse' is a fine orientation, but 'descending disc' describes a different thing. The part has no label, so a rule would need to separate anther dehiscence from disc position.
Fragile fits some delicate parts but not every part. Delicate or slender is a different sense. There is no part label.
Orbicular is a standard shape for flat parts.
'Ellipsoid' is not 'prolate'. Bracts are flat, so ellipsoid maps to elliptic. This is a wrong reading.
Bracts are often shorter than the spikes or the peduncle. The comparison is to another part, so the length is relative.
Papery or chartaceous bracts are common.
The ostiole has a diameter, and the examples are measurements.
Trichomes can be sparse. One example is about rhizome scales.
Measured lengths ('95-125 cm long') belong to length with a value. Only comparisons ('longer than the sterile ones') fit increased length. A rule would need to split measurements from comparisons.
'Hydathodes frequent' is about how frequent they are, so frequency fits.
Spotted or flecked leaves are a normal description.
Length measurements are meaningful for a measurable part.
A knobby stigma is meaningful and the examples are consistent.
Rose-coloured sepals are meaningful.
Semiglobose is a hemispheroid shape and the examples fit.
Nectary scales can be subulate. There is only one example.
A caruncle can be fimbriate.
Arilloids or pseudarils can be lobed, as the examples show.
'Solitary' is a count of awns per spikelet, not a spatial pattern. It belongs in a counted-parts rule.
The anther tube has a length, and the examples are measurements.
A hairless calyptra is a standard moss description.
A viscid hypanthium is meaningful, and the examples are consistent.
Lenticels can be erumpent, meaning protruding.
Cortex thickness is meaningful. The examples come from lichen text in Latin, so the part may be a lichen cortex rather than a plant cortex.
Flowers or floral cups can be sericeous (silky) in many floras.
'Sharp-pointed apex' describes the apex, not the whole bud scale. A rule would need to map apex shape to the apex part.
Buds can be hidden or concealed by leaves or petiole bases.
Pendent sepals are meaningful. One example is about a spur.
Bark can be coloured, and the examples are cinnamon-coloured bark. A specific colour term would be better if one exists.
